newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria blue-collar vote shifts to far right.
newsitem.headline: Austria blue-collar vote shifts to far right.

text.p: Austria's far right won huge support from blue-collar voters in a European election and Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's Social Democrats should heed their worries rather than brush them aside, analysts said on Monday.

The triumphant nationalist Freedom Party scored an all-time high in Sunday's election, pushing its support to 27.6 percent, just a few thousand votes behind the Social Democrats who slumped to an historic low on 29.1 percent.

The message from voters was two-fold -- they are angry at an austerity budget that has cut welfare benefits and raised taxes, largely to ensure Austria meets criteria set out in the Maastricht treaty for planned European economic integration and a single currency.

And the voters who backed the far right, many of them workers scared about their futures, are deeply worried that mounting job losses, and bankruptcies and takeovers will get worse as Austria integrates into the European Union.
"We have estimated that 50 percent of the blue-collar vote this time went to the Freedom Party," Rudolf Bretschneider, chief analyst at Vienna's Fessl research institute said.
"It is clear that scepticism over the EU has increased in Austria over the past two years," he told Reuters.

The fact that far-right leader Joerg Haider laces his Euro-scepticism with anti-immigrant invective makes his party's surge in popularity the more worrying, especially abroad, political analysts said.
The Social Democrats were complacent, believing they could always rely on the working class vote it has depended on for nearly 80 years, one analyst said.
But blue-collar support is leeching to the right, much as it did in Britain in 1979 when Margaret Thatcher won over voters traditionally loyal to the Labour Party, he said.

Vranitzky, a fiercely pro-European former banker, blamed his party's worst vote in Austrian democratic history on a low turnout, but said his government would press on with policies it knew were correct.

"The government should listen very carefully to the message from the voters," said Christina Matzka, an analyst with Austria's OGM political research institute. "The budget cuts are really hurting and people are linking it with the Maastricht criteria and our payments to Brussels."
Austria this year will make a net contribution of 15 billion schillings ($1.4 billion) to EU coffers.
"The high-profile cases of (tyre-maker) Semperit and (supermarket chain) Billa make people think the EU is buying up Austria," Matzka said.

Semperit's German parent Continental plans to move production from Austria to the Czech Republic to avoid high wage costs, cutting the 2,400-strong workforce by half. Billa was taken over by German supermarket giant Rewe in July.
An EU diplomatic source stressed that nearly 60 percent of the electorate backed pro-EU parties but acknowledged that Haider had become a conduit for a protest vote.

Vranitzky's junior coalition party, the conservative People's Party came out on top in the Euro-poll with 29.6 percent, largely due to popular candidates, including Karl Habsburg, the grandson of the last Austro-Hungarian emperor. But the party made few pledges it knew it could not keep.

"Vranitzky said money to pensioners would not be cut, but it was. The government said there would be more jobs, but people are believing Haider when he says none came and the EU is taking them away," Matzka said.
